title: Three-point shift handoff & p99 gardening
content:
Context:
- Night shift: covering midnight -> 08:00 PT. Quick log for handoff to morning team (Omar). Keep this rough; use as checklist and scratchpad.
- Primary focus last 12h: recurring p99 tail on model-x-v2 (decoder-only, 2.7B) when seq_len > 4k and concurrent sessions > 130.
- Symptoms: p99 token latency spikes (~1.4s -> 3.1s), KV cache thrash events, sporadic NVLink congestion reported in dmesg logs.

Immediate observations (raw):
- 2026-03-12T02:14:23Z  node-gpu-7  serving: request id=7c9f3b kv-evict "evicted 12 segments"
- 2026-03-12T02:14:23Z  node-gpu-7  nvlink: peer reset on link 1 (stats: rx=1.2M tx=0.9M)
- 2026-03-12T02:14:23Z  node-gpu-7  scheduler: batch_size mismatch target=16 actual=3 (lots of small batching)
- 2026-03-12T02:18:05Z  node-gpu-3  cpu-steal=3.7% during p99 spike window
- Traces show a cluster of requests with identical prefix hashes hitting same shard -> small-window hot-keys.

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) KV cache eviction storms from tiny TTL + high churn (many short-lived chat sessions) -> cache thrash + extra KV loads -> increased per-token compute and nvlink transfers.
2) Hot-sharding: prefix hashing mapped many live sessions to same GPU shard because of new routing policy introduced last week (policy v2) that prefers locality but didn't consider token-length distribution.
3) CUDA/NVLink transient overload when concurrent NVLink transfers spike due to KV fetches (observe nvlink resets).
4) Scheduler batching misprediction: warmup logic penalizes building larger batches for these prefixes, causing many tiny batches and per-token overhead.

Quick repro plan (cheap experiments):
- Toggle routing policy fallback to v1 for a 1-hour window on a canary pool and compare p99 (metric: token_latency.p99). (Owner: Omar; ETA: today 09:30)
- Increase KV per-session TTL from 60s -> 300s on dedicated model-x shards for 2h and measure eviction rate (metric: kv.evictions/sec). (Owner: me; ETA: rolling by 03:30)
- Force larger minimal batch size for model-x (min_batch=8) on canary 2 nodes to see batching effect. (Owner: Priya; ETA: 04:00)
- Temporarily enable detailed nvlink counters on node-gpu-7 for next 4h (low overhead). (Owner: infra-sre oncall; tag: s-ops)

Quick commands / breadcrumbs:
- tail -n 200 /var/log/serving/runtime.log | grep "kv-evict" -- context around 02:14
- ./bin/trace-query --id 7c9f3b --export traces/7c9f3b.json
- kubectl logs -n serving pod/node-gpu-7 -c runtime --since=3h | jq '.message' | grep nvlink
- redis-cli -h kv-store-3 INFO memory; redis-cli -h kv-store-3 SLOWLOG GET 50

Short-term mitigation (if spike worsens):
- Put model-x on overflow to model-x-quantized (lower bandwidth) using routing fallback policy for 30m rolling window.
- Reject new long-context sessions at edge with 503 + retry-advice when cluster concurrency > 150. (we already have a knob: serving.route/token_limit)

Open bugs / tickets to reference:
- RW-4982: kv eviction high-water edge case (linked) -- triaged as P2. Root cause analysis started.
- INF-349: scheduler warmup misprediction for decoder-only models (linear ref).
- GH PR #2103: kernel patch improves KV lookup async batching (need to land + benchmark).

Notes-to-self about kernel patch: GH#2103 changed the async_get path to batch remote KV requests for >4 keys. Need to confirm backpressure correctness: it uses in-flight-count limit=64; if we reduce to 32, might avoid NVLink bursts but increase latency for some workloads. Also check that the futures are drained in reverse order (we saw reordering artifact in traces).

Metrics snapshot (rough at 03:00):
- cluster token throughput: 1.2M tokens/min
- model-x QPS: 420 -> p50 token latency 110ms, p95 450ms, p99 3.1s
- kv.evictions/sec (cluster): baseline 2.1 -> spike 18.3 at 02:14
- nvlink errors last 24h: 4 resets (nodes: gpu-7,gpu-2)

To-do (short actionable list):
- [ ] Roll TTL bump to model-x dedicated shards (me) — verify eviction/sec drops below 5 within 30m.
- [ ] Coordinate with infra-sre to enable nvlink counters and check thermals (Omar).
- [ ] Run microbench: run replayer with 200 concurrent sessions, long-context (6k tokens) against model-x canary (Priya).
- [ ] Smoke test GH#2103 on staging, validate no reordering regressions (me + Priya).
- [ ] Add telemetry: tag requests with prefix-hash -> track shard concentration over last 24h (followup ticket).
- [ ] Draft short postmortem skeleton if TTL experiment doesn't fix within 6h (me).

Handoff notes for morning (Omar):
- If p99 still >2.2s after TTL bump, prioritize routing policy rollback (v2 -> v1) because v2's locality heuristic is likely colliding with long-context heavy sessions.
- Check the 'batch_miss_ratio' metric — big signal if >0.4 indicates scheduler failing to aggregate.
- Look for repeated 'prefix_hash=0xdeadbeef' in logs — I added a quick grep alias: grep "prefix_hash=0x" runtime.log | cut -d ' ' -f6 | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -n 20

Random notes / hypotheses to explore later:
- Could prefetching hot prefixes into local NVMe reduce NVLink bursts? Might help for stable long-lived chat sessions. Consider an LRU pinned set per-host.
- Evaluate whether TTL should be adaptive by session length distribution: e.g., TTL = base_ttl * sqrt(session_avg_len / 512).
- Investigate whether the new routing policy uses a consistent hashing salt that changed last week (check infra-config v2 change log).

Unresolved questions:
- Are the nvlink resets happening because of software driver in corner-case (e.g., peer reset due to a large pipeline transfer) or hardware flakiness? (Need infra diagnostics)
- Is the SDK client sending many small requests or are single large requests being split? Need to correlate client logs (CC-2316)

End-of-shift checklist (what I actually did):
- TTL experiment queued (rolling deploy to 2/6 shards) — started at 03:15, control=shard1,2; canary=shard3,4.
- Notified infra-sre about nvlink counters.
- Captured 3 full traces and uploaded to traces/ dir.
- Left quick PR comment on GH#2103 asking for in-order draining test.

If anything urgent ping me on slack @lexi (I will be online 06:30–07:30 PT before leaving).

-- scratchy and messy but keeping to the essentials; will flesh into a short incident note if TTL rollback or routing fallback needed.
